```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys, pathlib
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path.cwd() / "src"))
from lectures import plotting, datasets
from lectures.plotting import INK, COOL, WARM, CRASH, despine, annotate_box
from lectures.measures import cocrash_fraction
plotting.set_style("notes")
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import einx                      # linear algebra with the axes spelled out
from jaxtyping import Float      # shape annotations: Float[Array, "n_days"]
```

*Apply-the-tool track · Job A.*

A stress test is only as honest as the scenarios you feed it, and the dangerous
scenarios are the **joint** ones — the days when many stocks crash at the same
time.  A Gaussian stress engine keeps the correlation but shaves that joint tail
off, quietly understating the capital you would actually need.  (The "joint tail"
is just the rare corner where everything drops together; a Gaussian model makes
that corner look emptier than it really is.)  This lab builds a **stress set** the
right way: fit RBIG (Rotation-Based Iterative Gaussianization) forward so the real
returns become a standard Gaussian, then draw fresh Gaussian points and push them
back through the *inverse* map to get new return-like scenarios that keep the fat
joint tail.  The single fit-then-sample recipe is fixed on Rung 1 and reused
unchanged as the data grows up under it — from a 2-D pair whose answer we know, to
the real basket.

**What you will produce:** a stress set — a batch of synthetic (computer-generated)
joint scenarios whose co-crash structure (how often names crash together) and
worst-case joint loss match the real book and overshoot a Gaussian stress — the
input a risk engine needs, ready to hand to
[Job B · Portfolio VaR](lab-jobB-portfolio-var.qmd).

---

## 🧪 Rung 1 · Toy — Known Answer

Start where the truth is not in doubt.  `datasets.correlated_returns(rho=0.7)`
draws a **known** 2-D Gaussian pair: correlation $\rho = 0.7$ (the two assets move
together fairly strongly) and unit-variance marginals (each asset on its own has a
standard bell-curve shape), both quantities we can read straight off the generator.
A stress generator that is working must reproduce *both* — hand back the same
correlation and the same one-asset-at-a-time (marginal) shapes — and here we can
check each by hand.

```{python}
x_toy: Float[Array, "n"]
y_toy: Float[Array, "n"]
x_toy, y_toy = datasets.correlated_returns(n=3000, rho=0.7, seed=0)

X_toy: Float[Array, "n 2"] = np.column_stack([x_toy, y_toy])
X_toy = (X_toy - X_toy.mean(0)) / X_toy.std(0)        # zᵢ = (xᵢ − μ)/σ   (standardize → z-scores)


def pearson(z1: Float[Array, "n"], z2: Float[Array, "n"]) -> float:
    """Pearson correlation of two columns, axes spelled out.

    ρ = Σᵢ z̃₁ᵢ·z̃₂ᵢ / √(Σᵢ z̃₁ᵢ²·Σᵢ z̃₂ᵢ²),   z̃ = z − z̄   (mean-centered)
    """
    c1: Float[Array, "n"] = z1 - z1.mean()
    c2: Float[Array, "n"] = z2 - z2.mean()

    num = einx.dot("n, n ->", c1, c2)                          # Σᵢ z̃₁ᵢ·z̃₂ᵢ
    den = np.sqrt(einx.dot("n, n ->", c1, c1) * einx.dot("n, n ->", c2, c2))
    return float(num / den)


rho_true = pearson(X_toy[:, 0], X_toy[:, 1])          # ρ = Cov(z₁,z₂)/(σ₁·σ₂)
print(f"X_toy: {X_toy.shape}    known correlation ρ ≈ {rho_true:.3f}")
```

**The algorithm — fit forward, sample backward.**  Gaussianization learns an
invertible map $T$ with $T(\text{data}) \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I)$.  Generating a
fresh scenario is then just the inverse map applied to new Gaussian noise:

```
fit       T : data → z ~ N(0, I)        # RBIG, forward
sample    z ~ N(0, I)                   # draw in the easy space
generate  x = T⁻¹(z) ~ data             # inverse map → new return-like scenarios
```

`AnnealedRBIG.fit` learns $T$; `.sample(n)` does the draw-then-invert in one
call.  This is the *entire* stress generator — defined once here, reused on every
rung:

```{python}
from rbig import AnnealedRBIG


def fit_generate(data: Float[Array, "n d"], n_gen: int, seed: int = 0) -> Float[Array, "n_gen d"]:
    """Fit RBIG forward (data → Gaussian), then sample its INVERSE map.

    T : data → z ~ N(0, I)      learned by .fit         (forward Gaussianization)
    x = T⁻¹(z),  z ~ N(0, I)    produced by .sample(n)  (backward → new scenarios)
    """
    model = AnnealedRBIG(n_layers=30, rotation="pca", random_state=seed).fit(data)
    return model.sample(n_gen)                          # (n_gen, d) fresh scenarios


gen_toy: Float[Array, "n 2"] = fit_generate(X_toy, n_gen=3000, seed=0)
print(f"generated {gen_toy.shape[0]} scenarios with the same fit-then-sample recipe")
```

Now read the generated scenarios against what we *know* is there — the
correlation and the marginals:

```{python}
rho_gen = pearson(gen_toy[:, 0], gen_toy[:, 1])       # ρ of the generated cloud
print(f"correlation   true {rho_true:+.3f}   generated {rho_gen:+.3f}")
print(f"marginal std  true {X_toy.std(0).round(2)}   generated {gen_toy.std(0).round(2)}")
print(f"marginal mean true {X_toy.mean(0).round(2)}   generated {gen_toy.mean(0).round(2)}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-toy-roundtrip
#| fig-cap: "The known-answer round-trip. Left: the real ρ=0.7 cloud. Middle: RBIG-generated scenarios from the inverse map — same tilt, same spread. Right: the two marginal histograms of asset 1 overlaid; the generated marginal (orange) lands on the real one (blue). The stress generator reproduces both the correlation and the marginal shapes it was never told directly."
fig, (ax0, ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 4.2))
for ax, data, col, ttl in [(ax0, X_toy, COOL, f"real · ρ = {rho_true:.2f}"),
                           (ax1, gen_toy, WARM, f"generated · ρ = {rho_gen:.2f}")]:
    ax.scatter(data[:, 0], data[:, 1], s=8, c=col, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_xlim(-4, 4)
    ax.set_ylim(-4, 4)
    ax.set_xlabel("asset 1 (z)")
    ax.set_ylabel("asset 2 (z)")
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=11)
    despine(ax)

bins = np.linspace(-4, 4, 40)
ax2.hist(X_toy[:, 0], bins=bins, density=True, color=COOL, alpha=0.55, label="real")
ax2.hist(gen_toy[:, 0], bins=bins, density=True, color=WARM, alpha=0.55, label="generated")
ax2.set_title("asset 1 marginal", fontsize=11)
ax2.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False)
despine(ax2)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The known answer holds: the inverse map hands back the same $\rho \approx 0.7$ and
the same Gaussian marginals.  On a clean Gaussian there is nothing a covariance
stress would miss — the recipe is correct, so now we let the data get harder, into
exactly the territory a Gaussian stress *does* miss.

---

## 🎭 Rung 2 · Toy-Real — A Stylized Market

A clean Gaussian pair never happens in markets.  What *does* is a **co-crash**:
two names that drift together on calm days and plunge together on the bad ones,
with heavy tails (extreme moves that happen more often than a bell curve predicts)
that a Gaussian stress would shave off.  `datasets.tail_dependent_pair()` is a
simplified stand-in for that — a shared shock that hits both assets at once, giving
each one fat tails and making them especially likely to crash together.  We run the
**exact same** `fit_generate` and ask the question a stress test lives or dies on:
does the inverse map reproduce the lower-left corner where both assets crash at
once — the structure a Gaussian simulation would thin out?

```{python}
a: Float[Array, "n"]
b: Float[Array, "n"]
a, b = datasets.tail_dependent_pair(n=2000, df=3, seed=0)

X_pair: Float[Array, "n 2"] = np.column_stack([a, b])         # already standardized
cc_real = cocrash_fraction(X_pair[:, 0], X_pair[:, 1])        # P(both in worst 10%)
print(f"stylized co-crashing pair: {X_pair.shape}   real co-crash = {cc_real:.0%}")

gen_pair: Float[Array, "n 2"] = fit_generate(X_pair, n_gen=2000, seed=0)   # same recipe
cc_gen = cocrash_fraction(gen_pair[:, 0], gen_pair[:, 1])
```

A Gaussian stress fit to the same correlation is the benchmark to beat — it keeps
the overall tilt of the cloud (the two assets still move together) but thins out
the extreme corner, so its co-crash falls short of the real one:

```{python}
rho_pair = pearson(X_pair[:, 0], X_pair[:, 1])           # ρ of the real fat-tailed pair
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
g_pair: Float[Array, "n 2"] = rng.multivariate_normal(   # Gaussian stress, same ρ, unit variance
    [0, 0], [[1, rho_pair], [rho_pair, 1]], size=2000)
cc_gauss = cocrash_fraction(g_pair[:, 0], g_pair[:, 1])

print(f"{'source':<24}{'co-crash':>10}")
print("-" * 34)
print(f"{'real pair':<24}{cc_real:>10.0%}")
print(f"{'RBIG stress set':<24}{cc_gen:>10.0%}   ← inverse map keeps the joint tail")
print(f"{'Gaussian stress (same ρ)':<24}{cc_gauss:>10.0%}   ← thins it")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-pair-cocrash
#| fig-cap: "Regenerating the co-crash. Left: the real fat-tailed pair, lower-left co-crash quadrant shaded. Middle: RBIG-generated scenarios — the inverse map repacks the same lower-left corner, so its co-crash matches the real one. Right: a Gaussian stress with the identical correlation keeps the tilt but empties the corner, understating the joint tail. The fat-tail structure survives the backward map; it does not survive the Gaussian."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13.5, 4.6), sharex=True, sharey=True)
panels = [(X_pair, COOL, f"real · co-crash {cc_real:.0%}"),
          (gen_pair, WARM, f"RBIG stress set · co-crash {cc_gen:.0%}"),
          (g_pair, "0.5", f"Gaussian stress · co-crash {cc_gauss:.0%}")]
for ax, (data, col, ttl) in zip(axes, panels):
    qx, qy = np.quantile(data[:, 0], 0.10), np.quantile(data[:, 1], 0.10)  # 10% crash lines
    box: Float[Array, "n"] = (data[:, 0] <= qx) & (data[:, 1] <= qy)       # co-crash quadrant

    ax.axvspan(-8, qx, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06)
    ax.axhspan(-8, qy, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06)
    ax.scatter(data[~box, 0], data[~box, 1], s=6, c=col, alpha=0.25, edgecolors="none")
    ax.scatter(data[box, 0], data[box, 1], s=14, c=CRASH, alpha=0.7, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_xlim(-6, 5)
    ax.set_ylim(-6, 5)
    ax.set_xlabel("asset A (z)")
    ax.set_ylabel("asset B (z)")
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=11)
    despine(ax)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Two things to take away.  First, the RBIG scenarios match the real co-crash rate
while the Gaussian stress falls short — the inverse map carried the fat joint tail
across.  That is the whole point of stressing *through* a learned density (a model
of the full shape of the data) rather than through correlation alone.  Second, no
new code did this: the same `fit_generate` from Rung 1, the same `cocrash_fraction`.
Only the data got market-shaped.  Now the real book.

## 📈 Rung 3 · Real — The Full Basket

Now the real panel.  We **reload** the prepared returns — there is no cleaning
here.  The prices → log-returns pipeline and the co-crash structure these names
ride on already live in
[Co-Movement & Co-Crashes](../../data/04-co-movement-and-co-crashes.qmd).  We take
a real sub-basket that spans two sectors — two banks (JPM, BAC) and an energy major
(XOM), so there is a genuine cross-sector tail to stress — and run the *same*
`fit_generate`.

**What we are looking for:** for each pair of assets, the co-crash fraction — the
share of days both land in their worst 10% at once.  If the generator is honest,
the co-crash number it produces should match the real one for every pair,
*including* the bank-vs-energy pairs where a sector-blind model tends to miss the
shared crashes.

```{python}
R = datasets.load_returns()                       # prepared 14-name daily panel
assets = ["JPM", "BAC", "XOM"]                    # two banks + one energy → cross-sector tail
X_real: Float[Array, "n_days 3"] = R[assets].to_numpy()
X_real = (X_real - X_real.mean(0)) / X_real.std(0)   # zⱼ = (xⱼ − μⱼ)/σⱼ   (standardize columns → z-scores)
print(f"{len(X_real)} trading days × {len(assets)} names "
      f"({R.index.min().date()} → {R.index.max().date()})   assets = {assets}")
R[assets].head(3).round(4)
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Where This Data Comes From
The panel, its sectors, and the co-crash structure these scenarios must reproduce
are laid bare in the data primer —
[Co-Movement & Co-Crashes](../../data/04-co-movement-and-co-crashes.qmd).  This
lab reloads that panel and never re-derives it.
:::

RBIG is fit per-render, so we keep $n$ modest — a few thousand generated scenarios
is plenty for the tail statistics below.  Same recipe, real data:

```{python}
gen_real: Float[Array, "n_gen 3"] = fit_generate(X_real, n_gen=4000, seed=0)
print(f"generated {gen_real.shape[0]} three-asset scenarios from the real fit\n")

print(f"{'pair':<12}{'real co-crash':>14}{'generated':>12}")
print("-" * 38)
for i, j in [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2)]:
    cr = cocrash_fraction(X_real[:, i], X_real[:, j])
    cg = cocrash_fraction(gen_real[:, i], gen_real[:, j])
    print(f"{assets[i] + '/' + assets[j]:<12}{cr:>14.0%}{cg:>12.0%}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-real-scenarios
#| fig-cap: "Real returns (left) and RBIG-generated scenarios (right) for the JPM/BAC pair from the three-asset fit. The bulk cloud and the shaded lower-left co-crash quadrant match — the within-bank joint crash the basket is famous for survives the backward map. The generator was fit on all three names jointly, so the cross-sector XOM tail is preserved too (see the table above)."
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.6), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, data, col, ttl in [
    (axL, X_real, COOL, f"real · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(X_real[:, 0], X_real[:, 1]):.0%}"),
    (axR, gen_real, WARM, f"generated · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(gen_real[:, 0], gen_real[:, 1]):.0%}"),
]:
    qx, qy = np.quantile(data[:, 0], 0.10), np.quantile(data[:, 1], 0.10)  # 10% crash lines
    ax.axvspan(-8, qx, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06)
    ax.axhspan(-8, qy, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06)
    ax.scatter(data[:, 0], data[:, 1], s=7, c=col, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_xlim(-6, 5)
    ax.set_ylim(-6, 5)
    ax.set_xlabel("JPM (z)")
    ax.set_ylabel("BAC (z)")
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=11)
    despine(ax)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The real basket behaves like the stylized pair, only messier: every pairwise
co-crash in the generated set tracks the real one, including the cross-sector
JPM/XOM tail that a sector-blind correlation model would smooth away.  The
generator preserves the dangerous structure on data it was never told the
structure of — which is exactly the property a stress set is supposed to have.

## 💰 Rung 4 · Application — The Stress Set

The deliverable is a **stress set**: a batch of generated joint scenarios shipped
with the tail statistics that justify trusting it.  A stress set is only useful if
it carries the *dangerous* structure, so we score it on exactly that — against the
real book and against the Gaussian stress it is meant to replace.

**The two numbers we read:** (1) the average co-crash fraction across all asset
pairs — how often, on average, two names crash together; and (2) the **worst-case
joint loss** — the single worst day for an equal-weight portfolio (hold the same
amount of each name) that each source produces.  If the inverse map preserved the
joint tail, both numbers should match the real data and overshoot the Gaussian:
the RBIG stress set should look as dangerous as reality, while the Gaussian stress
looks too calm.

```{python}
def worst_joint_loss(data: Float[Array, "n d"]) -> float:
    """Most negative equal-weight portfolio return — the worst single day.

    pₜ = (1/d) Σⱼ data[t, j]      equal-weight book           [z-score units]
    loss = minₜ pₜ                the worst joint draw (a co-crash day)
    """
    port: Float[Array, "n"] = einx.mean("t d -> t", data)     # pₜ = (1/d)·Σⱼ data[t,j]
    return float(port.min())


def mean_cocrash(data: Float[Array, "n d"]) -> float:
    """Average pairwise co-crash fraction over all asset pairs."""
    d = data.shape[1]
    pairs = [(i, j) for i in range(d) for j in range(i + 1, d)]
    return float(np.mean([cocrash_fraction(data[:, i], data[:, j]) for i, j in pairs]))


# Gaussian stress on the real covariance — the thin-tailed engine we are replacing.
n_real = X_real.shape[0]
Xc_real: Float[Array, "n_days 3"] = X_real - X_real.mean(0)              # x̃ = x − x̄   (mean-centered)
cov_real: Float[Array, "3 3"] = einx.dot("day i, day j -> i j", Xc_real, Xc_real) / (n_real - 1)   # Σ = (1/(n−1))·X̃ᵀX̃
g_real: Float[Array, "n_gen 3"] = np.random.default_rng(0).multivariate_normal(
    np.zeros(3), cov_real, size=4000)

print(f"{'source':<22}{'mean co-crash':>14}{'worst joint loss':>18}")
print("-" * 54)
for name, data in [("real book", X_real), ("RBIG stress set", gen_real),
                   ("Gaussian stress", g_real)]:
    print(f"{name:<22}{mean_cocrash(data):>14.0%}{worst_joint_loss(data):>18.2f}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-stress-set
#| fig-cap: "The stress set, scored on its danger. Left: average pairwise co-crash — the RBIG scenarios (orange) sit on the real book (blue) while the Gaussian stress (grey) falls short. Right: the distribution of equal-weight portfolio returns, left tail in focus; the RBIG tail reaches the real worst-case losses (dashed lines), the Gaussian tail stops short. The stress set preserves the joint extremes a covariance-based engine structurally misses."
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.6))

# Left: mean pairwise co-crash, three sources.
names = ["real book", "RBIG\nstress set", "Gaussian\nstress"]
sources = [X_real, gen_real, g_real]
cols = [COOL, WARM, "0.6"]
ccs = [mean_cocrash(s) for s in sources]

axL.bar(names, [c * 100 for c in ccs], color=cols)
axL.axhline(10, color=INK, lw=1.1, ls="--", label="independent baseline (10%)")
axL.set_ylabel("mean pairwise co-crash (%)")
axL.set_title("RBIG keeps the joint tail; the Gaussian thins it", fontsize=11)
axL.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False)
despine(axL)

# Right: equal-weight portfolio-return distributions, tail in focus.
bins = np.linspace(-5, 3, 60)
for data, col, name in [(X_real, COOL, "real"), (gen_real, WARM, "RBIG"), (g_real, "0.6", "Gaussian")]:
    port: Float[Array, "n"] = einx.mean("t d -> t", data)     # pₜ = (1/d)·Σⱼ data[t,j]
    axR.hist(port, bins=bins, density=True, histtype="step", lw=1.8, color=col, label=name)
    axR.axvline(port.min(), color=col, lw=1.0, ls="--", alpha=0.8)   # worst joint loss

axR.set_xlim(-5, 3)
axR.set_xlabel("equal-weight portfolio return (z)")
axR.set_ylabel("density")
axR.set_title("Portfolio loss tail — RBIG reaches the real worst case", fontsize=11)
axR.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False)
despine(axR)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The stress set passes its own test: its average co-crash and worst-case joint loss
sit on the real book, while the Gaussian stress — given the *exact* same
correlations — understates both.  The reason is simple: the joint extremes live in
a fat tail that correlation alone cannot capture.  The `gen_real` matrix is the
deliverable: a synthetic batch that carries the real dangerous structure, ready to
feed any portfolio risk function.

Where this hands off: a stress set is the *input*, not the answer.  Turning these
scenarios into a capital number — the 1% portfolio VaR (Value at Risk: the loss
the portfolio should exceed only 1% of the time), and the gap between the RBIG and
Gaussian stresses in dollars — is the job
[Job B · Portfolio VaR](lab-jobB-portfolio-var.qmd) takes up next.
